A06:
You leave your bag. It's a stupid thing to do in an airport and you do it anyway, because the last of them is already turning the corner, and Sam is asleep, and you are, it turns out, still the kind of person who goes.

The corridor past the toilets is long and carpeted and smells of mop buckets. *EXIT*, say the green signs, one after another, each little running man the same distance ahead of you as the last. You can hear the crowd in front. Shoes. The tick of a suitcase wheel with a stone caught in it. You can't see them.

The corridor bends left, and left again. A walkway hums alongside you, empty, carrying nothing anywhere at a steady walking pace. You keep off it without knowing why.

Left again.

You come out under a sign that says *Gate 14*.

The seats. The kiosk with its shutter down. Your bag, where you left it, its strap hanging off the armrest at the same lazy angle. Sam, asleep, chin on his chest, one empty seat away from yours.

The crowd is gone. Not further down the concourse. Not in the toilets. Gone, the way a sound is gone after it stops.

Three left turns have brought you back to where you started. It should take four. Gain 1 Fear.

You sit down next to your bag because your legs have decided it for you. Above the gate desk, without a sound, the number on the sign begins to change.

Turn to {A08}.
A07:
You stay.

The last of the crowd turns the corner and the sound of their feet goes with them. Then it's just you, the hum of a drinks fridge somewhere, and your brother breathing slowly through his nose.

Far down the concourse, a bank of lights goes out.

*Clunk.* The heavy, final sound of a breaker being thrown. Gate 22 is gone, then 21. *Clunk.* The dark comes up the concourse towards you one gate at a time.

*Clunk.* Gate 20. And nothing. It stops.

Gate 19 is the furthest gate still lit, five gates away. The tall passenger is standing in it, right at the edge of the light, as if the dark rolled up to its heels and politely waited.

It is holding up its sign. Too far away to read. Its arms must ache by now, you think, stupidly. It has been holding that sign up all night.

And every light goes out, yours included.

In the black, Sam jerks awake beside you with a gasp. He slaps at the empty seat between you, feeling for your arm. "What's happening? Who turned the—"

*Clunk.* The lights come back.

The tall passenger is standing at Gate 17.

Two gates closer. You didn't see it move. It holds its sign a little higher than before.

Turn to {A08}.
A08:
The sign above the gate desk doesn't say 14 any more.

It says *0*. Just that. A white zero on a blue panel, in the same rounded airport lettering as everything else, as though it has always said 0 and you're the one who has misremembered.

Sam is on his feet. You didn't see him get up. His earbuds hang loose round his neck, playing tinny music you almost recognise, and he is shaking. Not shivering. Shaking, the whole of him.

"Where is everyone?" he says. "The cleaner was right there. There were people. Where is everyone?"

He turns a full circle, and the departures board clatters over his head, every flap flipping in a blur of letters. He flinches.

"Did you see that? Did you see what it said?"

You didn't. It's back to *LV 137. DELAYED.*

He's gulping air. You know this. You knew it when he was eight and froze at the top of the climbing frame, and you talked him down one bar at a time.

You also know he hasn't let you touch him in three years. At the bag drop this morning he kept his fists jammed in his jacket, so you wouldn't try.

He's looking at you now. Properly, for the first time all day, as if you will know what this is.

If you take hold of Sam's arm and keep your voice low and steady, turn to {A09}.

If you tell Sam to calm down and stop overreacting, turn to {A10}.
A09:
You take his arm. Just above the elbow, the way you'd steady someone on ice.

He lets you.

"Hey," you say. "Hey. Look at me. We're all right. It's an airport. It's a broken airport in the middle of the night, and we're all right."

None of that is true, and he knows it, and it doesn't matter, because it's the voice. The voice from the top bunk, after the landing light went off, when he asked what was under the bed and you told him it was only suitcases. You haven't used it in years. You didn't know you had it any more.

He slows. The shaking goes out of his arm in stages, until it's just an arm, and your grip on it.

He leans in close.

"I saw Dad's name," he whispers. "On the board. Just now, where the flight should be. I saw his name."

You don't let go. He doesn't ask you to. Note the codeword THAW.

Behind you, at the gate desk that was empty a moment ago, someone politely clears their throat.

Turn to {A11}.
A10:
"Sam. Calm down. You're overreacting."

It comes out in Dad's tone. The flat, end-of-the-day one he used when a conversation was over. You hear it leave your mouth and you can't call it back.

Sam stops shaking. He goes completely still, and then he nods, once, as if you've confirmed something he already suspected.

"Right," he says. "Course. You'd know. You've been here the whole time."

He walks away to the big window where the runway should be. The glass shows nothing but black and the faint reflection of the two of you, and he stands there with his back to you, jabbing at a phone on three per cent, with no signal.

You think of three things to say. Each of them, in your head, comes out in Dad's tone. You say none of them.

A soft chime sounds from somewhere above. Smaller than the PA. The sound a call button makes on a plane, when someone in a seat needs attention.

Sam doesn't turn round. You follow him anyway, and stop short of him, and that is when you see that someone is at the gate desk, expecting you both.

Turn to {A11}.
A11:
She is standing behind the gate desk as if she has been there all night and you simply hadn't looked.

Navy uniform, red piping at the collar and cuffs, a silk scarf knotted at the throat. The cut is wrong for now: the shoulders too square, the skirt too long, a holiday-brochure uniform from before you could read. A pin on her lapel says *LARKVALE AIRWAYS*. Her name badge says *HOSTESS*. Not a name. Just that.

She is smiling. Every tooth in its place.

Her eyes are terrified.

They're huge and wet and they flick to you, to Sam, to the dark at the far end of the concourse, and back. Her mouth goes on smiling through all of it.

"Good evening," she says, and then, a half-second late, as if fetched from somewhere: nothing. No *sir*, no *madam*. "On behalf of Larkvale Airways, I'm so sorry for tonight's delay. May I offer you a complimentary refreshment voucher?" She settles at the keyboard. "I'll just need your name." Then, without looking away from you: "And the window seat for your brother, of course. He always has the window."

Sam says nothing. You can't tell whether her face is saying *please* or *don't*.

If you accept the voucher and give her your name, turn to {A12}.

If you smile back and politely refuse, turn to {A13}.

If you ask her how you get out of here, turn to {A14}.
A12:
You tell her your name. She waits after it, keys untouched, and the silence is the kind you fill, so you keep going until she starts.

She types it, humming. A pop song, years out of date, the one that was on every radio the winter you were six. Each key makes a hard plastic clack, too loud, and beneath the desk a printer wakes and begins to chatter.

Not a modern printer. The old kind, with holes down the sides of the paper. It goes on longer than any voucher should take.

"Hey," Sam says, sharp enough to carry, like a warning that has arrived too late.

The slip she tears off is pink, its perforated edge furred. *LARKVALE AIRWAYS. REFRESHMENT VOUCHER.* Your name runs across it in capitals, spelled right first time. Underneath:

*VALID UNTIL DEPARTURE. DO NOT LEAVE THE TERMINAL.*

"Thank you so much," she says. Tears spill down her cheeks. The smile doesn't move.

Note the VOUCHER on your Adventure Sheet. Add 1 to your Claim.

Far away, faintly, you hear a pen squeak against card. One letter. Then nothing.

When you look up from the slip, the desk is empty.

Turn to {A15}.
A13:
"No, thank you," you say. "We're fine."

"Of course." The smile doesn't flicker. "Of course you are."

She types anyway, humming an old tune. Clack. Clack. Clack. Two fingers, hunting for each letter and finding it, the way Dad used to type. You haven't told her anything. You count the keystrokes, and the number is right. It is the number of letters in your name.

Behind her, on the dead monitor bolted to the wall, green letters appear on the black, one at a time.

Your name, spelled the way your passport spells it.

It sits there a moment. It fades from the left, letter by letter: read, and put away for later.

"Noted," says the Hostess brightly. Her cheeks are wet.

Sam has come up close behind you, not touching. "How does she know that?" he says, and it isn't really a question. Gain 1 Fear.

When you look back at the desk, she's gone. The monitor is dark. The keyboard is warm.

Turn to {A15}.
A14:
"How do we get out?" you ask. "The exit. The real one. Back through to arrivals."

For the first time, a muscle moves in her face that isn't part of the smile. She glances at Sam. Back to you.

"All passengers must remain airside until boarding," she says. The words come out smooth and worn, said ten thousand times. "The Handbook is quite clear."

"What handbook?"

She doesn't answer. But her gaze drops, so slightly you might have imagined it, to the row of seats beside you. To the floor beneath them. Then up again, wide and wet and frantic.

"Have a pleasant flight," she says.

She steps out from behind the desk and walks away down the concourse. Her heels are the hard, narrow kind. You watch them strike the tiles where the carpet ends: once, twice, ten times.

They make no sound at all.

Sam watches her until she turns the corner. "Okay," he says. "Okay. I'm going to need someone to tell me that's normal."

You don't.

Turn to {A15}.
A15:
In the silence she leaves behind, Sam sits down hard on the nearest seat and puts his head down. He stays bent over, staring at the floor between his trainers.

"There's something under here," he says.

It's taped to the underside of the seat, the tape gone yellow and brittle. He peels it free and passes it to you without sitting up. A laminated booklet, the size of a safety card, its corners worn soft by handling. Larkvale navy, a thin red stripe, and in white capitals:

*IRREGULAR OPERATIONS HANDBOOK. LV 137 CREW. EDITION 1998.*

You read it again. LV 137. Your flight. Tonight's flight, sitting on the board as *DELAYED*. Why would tonight's flight have a crew handbook from 1998?

Inside, under a heading that says *SECTION 9: CONDUCT DURING EXTENDED GROUND DELAY*, the rules are typed on an old machine, the letters slightly uneven. Someone has gone over every one of them in biro, pressing so hard the laminate is dented.

*Crew must observe the following at all times and ensure that passengers do likewise.*

*1. Do not look at the passenger when the lights flicker.*

*2. Never answer the Announcer. Never give your name.*

*3. Never ride a walkway that runs backwards.*

*4. Do not eat or drink airside after midnight.*

*5. Gate 00 does not exist.*

*6. Do not sleep airside.*

*7. If something is wrong, turn back.*

The last page has been torn out. Not neatly. A ragged stub of laminate is left in the staples, as if whoever did it was in a hurry, or shaking.

Note the HANDBOOK on your Adventure Sheet. Its rules are printed on the back of the sheet. You will want them by heart.

Behind you, Sam gets up. You feel him lean over your shoulder, and you hear the moment he reaches rule one, because he stops breathing.

Turn to {A16}.
A16:
"*The passenger,*" Sam says, close to your ear. He taps rule one. "Not passengers. One. Whoever wrote this was scared of someone specific."

His eyes go down the list and stop.

"*Do not sleep airside.*" He laughs, a thin sound. "I haven't slept since March. Let them try."

The laugh goes out of him.

"Except I did," he says. "Before. I don't even remember being tired."

"You were only out a few minutes."

"Was I?" He's looking at the rule, not at you. "Felt longer. And someone was sitting next to me. I felt the row move when they sat down."

You both look at the empty seat. The one between yours and his, that neither of you put a bag on. That nobody sat in.

The booklet is light, and it is the only solid thing in the building. Sam is watching you for a decision. You've got out of practice.

If you go through it with Sam, reading it aloud together cover to cover, turn to {A17}.

If you put it in your pocket and get the two of you moving, turn to {A18}.
A17:
You read it aloud, the two of you, a rule each. Your voice, then his. One to seven.

Inside the back cover, where the torn page used to face it, someone has scratched words into the laminate with the point of a biro, gouging so deep the letters show white:

*RULE 0. IT KEEPS THE ONES WHO NEVER SAID GOODBYE.*

Beneath it, in different writing, someone wrote a line and then scribbled it out. Hard, back and forth, until the pen went through. Only three words in the middle survive:

*…WHERE ONE WAS…*

Sam tilts the booklet to the light. "Where one was what?"

You've no idea. You read Rule 0 again instead.

You know you're both thinking of the same room. A bedroom in a house you haven't been back to. A phone buzzing on a table in another country, at an hour you let it ring.

"I did," Sam says at last. "Every time I went out the front door. *Bye, Dad.*" A sound that is nearly a laugh. "He'd shout back, *Mind how you go.* Even when I was only doing the bins."

He doesn't ask whether you did.

Sam closes the booklet and presses it back on you. "Keep that somewhere safe," he says. Lose 1 Fear.

Above you, one of the long ceiling tubes begins to buzz.

Turn to {A18}.
A18:
You have the Handbook in your pocket and Sam on his feet, and you've barely started down the concourse, when the lights stutter.

Off, on, off. The tubes buzz like flies in a jar.

In the dark between flickers you see nothing at all.

In the light, you see the tall passenger.

It is much nearer than when you last saw it, and you never saw it move. It's standing between the rows of seats, facing you. It holds its sign up in front of its chest with both arms. Or more than both. The light doesn't stay on long enough for you to count.

Off. On. It hasn't moved.

Off.

Behind you, Sam's breath catches and holds.

You know the first rule without looking. *Do not look at the passenger when the lights flicker.*

But the trouble with not looking is that you don't know where it is.

On. It's closer.

If you keep your eyes on it, turn to {A19}.

If you squeeze your eyes shut, turn to {A20}.
A19:
You look.

Off, on, off, on, you stare until it stings. Every time the light comes back it is a little nearer, and every time you see one thing more.

It is taller than one person should be. The long coat hangs from shoulders that don't sit level: the left one high, the right one lower, and, lower again beneath that, a third. The cloth moves when nothing else does.

Too many hands hold the sign. You count six before you make yourself stop. One of them is small. A child's hand, with a plaster round one finger, gripping the card as hard as the others.

The sign is old card, gone soft. It is covered in names. Dozens of them, in different writing, each crossed out with one neat line.

At the bottom, in fresh black marker, still wet: the beginning of your name.

Above the collar there is a face. The light goes before you can see whose.

A pain wrenches behind your face, as if the looking is being pulled out of you by the roots. Your mouth tastes of coins. Lose 2 Vigour. Gain 2 Fear. Add 1 to your Claim.

Off.

On. It's gone. Sam is dragging you down behind the seats with his arm across your face. "Don't look," he keeps saying. "Don't look. I've got it. I've got you."

Turn to {A21}.
A20:
You shut your eyes.

Every animal part of you wants to see. You screw them shut so tight you see colours, and the lights go on flickering through your eyelids: red, black, red.

The flickering stops, and it stays black. The dark is outside your eyelids now, not behind them. You can tell the difference.

You hear it coming: the soft drag of a long coat across carpet. And breathing. A great deal of breathing, many breaths, slightly out of time with each other, like a choir that has never rehearsed. In, in, in. Out. In. Out, out.

It passes close. Close enough that the air moves against your cheek. Close enough to smell: wet wool, old carpet, and underneath, faint, somebody's aftershave.

You keep them shut.

Something in the dark takes hold of you. You nearly scream. You know the grip: warm, shaking, the nails bitten down to nothing. Sam, holding on.

The breathing moves away down the concourse. In, in, out. Fainter. Gone.

The lights come back. Sam looks before you do.

*If you have THAW,* he's the one who says it, in the voice from the top bunk: "Only suitcases." Then, hoarse: "Your turn to believe it."

Turn to {A21}.
A21:
*If you have been here before:* the gate clock is ticking over the desk again. Go straight to the choices at the end of this section.

The lights hold. Steady, white, humming. Whatever passed, it isn't here now.

"We're not staying here," Sam says, and for once you agree with him without arguing first.

You walk. Away from the dark end of the concourse, past the kiosk, past the toilets, following signs that say *ALL GATES* with an arrow pointing where you're already heading. The corridor curves. You come out into a gate area. Your gate area.

You take it in properly. Four rows of grey plastic seats, bolted together in sixes. A cleaning cart parked at the end of the second row: yellow bucket, grey mop, a bin bag tied off.

The kiosk, shutter down. The gate desk and its dead monitor. A charging point with a cable plugged in and no phone on the end of it. The window, black. The board: *LV 137. DELAYED.*

And above the desk, the gate clock, big and round and white, the kind they hang in school halls. Its thin red pointer clicks round, steady. Eleven. Ten. Nine. Eight.

Sam has stopped beside you. "Is this ours?" he says. "It can't be the same one. We walked away from it."

The seventh rule is in your pocket. *If something is wrong, turn back.*

Is something wrong here? Or is it just an airport, built the same all the way down?

If you think something is wrong, and turn back the way you came, turn to {A22}.

If you think nothing is wrong, and keep walking through, turn to {A23}.
A22:
You turn round, back the way you came.

"What are you doing?" Sam says. "That's back towards it."

"The clock," you say. "It's going backwards."

He looks. You hear him take a breath and not let it out.

You walk back round the curve, and the corridor lets you go. No lurch. No folding. Just carpet and humming lights, and then the gate area again: the cleaning cart, the cable, the black window.

The clock. Its red pointer climbs from the six to the seven to the eight. Forwards. Ordinary.

Sam huffs through his nose, almost a laugh. "How did you see that? I was looking right at it."

"Spot the difference," you say. "You were always rubbish at it."

"I was always letting you win."

"You were rubbish at it."

He nearly smiles. Lose 1 Fear.

Above you, the PA chimes its two soft notes.

Turn to {A24}.
A23:
You keep walking: through the gate area, past the cleaning cart, past the cable with no phone on it, out the far side where the signs say *ALL GATES*. The corridor curves.

Halfway round the curve, the floor tilts. The lurch of a lift starting, or a plane dropping through a pocket of air: your stomach going one way and the rest of you the other. Sam grabs at a handrail you're fairly sure wasn't there a moment ago.

You come out into a gate area.

Four rows of grey seats. A cleaning cart. A yellow bucket. The cable. The black window. *LV 137. DELAYED.*

"No," Sam says. "No, no. We walked *away* from this."

You look at the clock. You looked at it last time, and it was just a clock. Now you see it: the red pointer clicking round from the eleven, to the ten, to the nine. It was doing that before. You looked straight at it and didn't see.

The airport showed you, and you missed it, and it let you go round again. It is patient. So far, that is the worst thing about it. Gain 1 Fear.

Somewhere above the black window, the PA clears its throat.

Turn to {A24}.
A24:
*Ding-dong.*

The two soft notes again, and then the small rustle of someone leaning in close to a microphone.

*Paging passenger…*

And it says your name.

Not the short one on your work email or your door buzzer. Your full name, every part, the middle one included, the one you only hear at the doctor's. The voice takes its time over each piece of it, kindly, as if handing it back to you.

You know the voice. Almost. It's smooth and kind and practised, never in a hurry, the voice of someone who has said these words a thousand times and meant them every time. Something in it tugs at you, the way a grown-up's voice did when you were small and safe and nearly asleep. You can't place it. You can almost place it.

*…please make yourself known to a member of staff.*

Sam is staring up at the speaker in the ceiling. "Is that…" he says, and doesn't finish.

*Please make yourself known,* the voice says again, gently. *We're all waiting for you.*

It would be so easy. Two words. It's what you're supposed to say when someone calls your name.

If you answer, "I'm here," turn to {D01}.

If you say nothing, turn to {A25}.
D01:
"I'm here," you say.

*Thank you,* says the voice, and it is so pleased. It comes from every speaker. From the dead monitor. From Sam's earbuds, dangling round his neck. Then from closer. From your chest. From behind your teeth.

*Thank you for making yourself known.*

Your jaw opens on its own, and your name comes out of it in that rough, kind voice, over and over, without stopping for breath, because you no longer need breath.

Somewhere far away Sam is shouting the short version, and you can't reach it. It's on the other side of your own mouth.

In the morning, the cleaners hear it on the PA, softly, between announcements: a name, repeated at a polite volume, by a voice that sounds as if it is smiling. They report it as a fault.

Maintenance closes the ticket. *NO FAULT FOUND.* The name goes on.

Add 1 to your Claim. Return to {A21} and choose again.
A25:
You say nothing. You press your lips together until they hurt.

The voice holds. You can hear it: the faint hiss of an open microphone, and somebody breathing close to it. Many somebodies.

*Ding-dong.*

*Paging passenger…*

Sam's name. The long one off his passport, the one only teachers and hospital receptions ever used.

Sam goes rigid beside you.

*Your family is waiting for you at Gate 0,* says the voice, and it is so kind. *They've been waiting such a long time. Please make yourself known.*

You turn to him. His face has gone slack, the way faces go in the moment before sleep. He is staring at the speaker, wet-faced. "I know that voice," he whispers.

His lips are starting to move. You can see the shape his mouth is making.

It's the shape of an *h*.

If you clap your hand over Sam's mouth, turn to {A26}.

If you let Sam answer, turn to {A27}.
A26:
Your hand is over his mouth. You don't remember moving it.

His whole body jerks, and for one horrible second he fights you, both arms coming up to tear your wrist away.

He freezes. You watch it arrive in his face: the speaker, the voice, the second rule. *Never answer the Announcer.* He understands.

The voice waits. The open microphone hisses. Somewhere far away a pen is lifted, and held, and not put down.

*Ding-dong,* says the PA at last, softly, almost disappointed, and then silence.

You let go. Sam steps back from you. His face is white and furious and his mouth is open to shout at you, and he doesn't. He wipes his mouth on his sleeve.

*If you have THAW,* the fury goes out of him as fast as it came. "Good," he says, hoarse. "Do that again. Any time I'm stupid."

Whatever he does, note the codeword CARE.

A long way off, a single light comes on.

Turn to {A28}.
A27:
You don't move fast enough. Or you don't move at all. Afterwards, you're never sure which.

"Here," Sam says.

It's barely a whisper. It's enough.

Every light in the terminal goes out with a sound like a breath being drawn in. And in the black, so close it might be beside his ear, you hear a pen. Scratching. One letter, in slow, careful strokes, the felt tip squeaking on card. Then another.

You grab him. You get your arms round his chest from behind and drag him backwards, his heels skidding on the carpet, until your shoulder slams into a cold, square edge. A pillar. You pull him down behind it and hold on.

It comes past. It's heavy. You feel it through the floor, through your knees: a slow weight, the carpet creaking under it. It stops on the other side of the pillar. You hear many breaths. You hear it, politely, wait.

Sam is shaking so hard that your teeth rattle. You press your face into the back of his neck and clamp your arm over his mouth now, now that it's too late, and hold on. It moves on.

When the lights come back, your forearms are bruised in long red bands where Sam's fingers dug in, and your shoulder screams. Lose 3 Vigour. Note the codeword MARKED.

Sam is staring at the back of his hand. There's a smudge of black ink on it, the blurred shape of a letter. He rubs at it. He spits on it and rubs harder. It doesn't come off.

A long way off, a single light comes on.

Turn to {A28}.
A28:
The light is a long way off: the far end of the concourse in the other direction, where the corridor opens into some larger space you can't see the shape of. Everything between here and there is dark. And out there, one pool of light.

You walk towards it because there is nothing else to walk towards. Sam keeps beside you.

As you get nearer, you see the light is coming from an information desk: a round counter under a tall glowing *i*, the only thing in the building that seems to be switched on properly. A screen is set into the counter, bright and blue.

Ten metres past it, half in the glow and half out, is the Larkvale Airways service desk. No lamp there. But someone is sitting behind it. You can make out the shape of a head, bowed. Shoulders. An arm resting on the counter.

"Information," Sam says under his breath. "That's what we need. Information."

The figure at the service desk doesn't lift its head. You realise you've been expecting it to, and that it isn't going to, and that it isn't asleep.

If you go to the information desk, turn to {A29}.

If you go to the airline service desk, turn to {A30}.
A29:
The information desk is unmanned. The swivel chair is pushed back, and there's a mug beside the keyboard with a skin on the tea.

The screen wakes as your shadow falls across it. *WELCOME*, it says, in Larkvale navy, and then a map unfolds.

It's the terminal, drawn in clean flat colours. From the centre, the airport branches into three zones, each labelled in tidy capitals. *THE CONCOURSE*. *DUTY-FREE & FOOD COURT*. *THE AIRPORT HOTEL*, reached by a skybridge drawn in a single fine line.

And at the centre, where all three meet, a gate pulses. Slow and steady, like an animal breathing in its sleep.

*GATE 0.*

You touch it. Nothing happens. You try to zoom out, to find the exits, the arrivals hall, the car parks. There aren't any. The map stops at its own edges.

Sam finds a slot under the counter and a button marked *PRINT*. The paper copy slides out, curling at the edges. Gate 0 is printed darker than everything else, gone over again and again.

Note the MAP on your Adventure Sheet.

"Look," Sam says. He points, not quite steadily, at the glass.

A small red dot says *YOU ARE HERE*. It isn't at the information desk. It's sitting in the middle of the map, on Gate 0, and it's blinking.

Turn to {A31}.
A30:
The figure behind the service desk was a man once. Grey skin, grey cardigan, grey hair combed down for a journey he set out on a long time ago.

The chair has grown over him. The upholstery has crept up his thighs and his back, and his wrists have gone into the armrests. A boarding card in his breast pocket has faded nearly white: *LV 137*.

"Is he…" Sam whispers.

The man's lips move before any sound comes, as if he began this sentence years ago and is only now arriving at the end of it.

"…not hers…" he says.

His chin dips to the card in his pocket. Then to the desk. Under his fused knuckles lies a passport, swollen and soft at the corners, and beside it a page of lined notepaper torn from a pad, a few words on it in faint pencil that you can't make out.

"…should have kept…"

His lids lift, wet and colourless, and find you. "When it wears someone… you love…" A breath that rattles all the way down, and nothing more comes.

His eyes close. The chair takes a little more of him.

When you reach for the notepaper, his knuckles close over it, slow as a tide. You leave it.

Sam reaches out to him and stops short. Neither of you touches him.

Turn to {A31}.
A31:
*If you have been here before:* the walkway is humming down the corridor again. Go straight to the choices at the end of this section.

Sam is shaking.

He's held it together, more or less, since the gate. Now it goes, like a dropped tray. He sits down on the floor with his back against the counter, pulls his knees up, puts his forehead on them.

He isn't crying. He's shaking, a fine fast tremor you can see in the zip of his jacket.

"Sorry," he says into his knees. "Give me a sec. I'm fine."

He has said *fine* to you a great many times, by text, in three years.

You crouch down, an arm's length away.

From further along the corridor, past the edge of the light, comes a low electric hum. Steady. Something moving, carrying nothing.

If you sit down on the floor beside Sam and let him rest a while, turn to {A32}.

If you get him back on his feet and keep moving, turn to {A33}.
A32:
You sit down beside him on the carpet, not quite touching him.

For a while neither of you speaks. The shaking slows.

"He was born in 1952," Sam says eventually. "'The year the old terminal opened.' He used to say it as if they'd built it for him."

"Every time we drove past."

"Every single time." Something that is nearly a laugh.

"He never flew again after '98. Never said why." Sam picks at a thread on his knee.

A memory stirs, far back. A phone held to your ear, too big for you. A kitchen at night. You, crying too hard to get the words out. It's gone before you can catch hold of it.

"I used to sit on the sofa and listen to you two talk about the weather." He laughs, short. "Brave man, Dad. Scared of a phone call."

You think of those calls. The weather, over there. You, telling him about the weather, and nothing else.

"He asked for you. 'Where's Kite flown off to now?'" He doesn't say what he told him. "I gave the flat up in May. Didn't see the point paying for a bed I wasn't in."

You never saw the flat.

He has stopped shaking. So have you. Gain 2 Vigour.

Sam stands.

*If you have THAW,* he picks up your bag as well as his own and waits, ready, the way he used to at the bottom of the viewing-deck stairs.

Turn to {A34}.
A33:
"Come on," you say. "We can't stop here." You get him up, and he lets you, and doesn't argue, which is how you know how bad it is.

The hum grows louder as you go. The corridor narrows, the ceiling drops, and there it is: a moving walkway, a long ribbon of grey rubber between two steel handrails, stretching away into the half-dark. The handrail ticks gently as it slides.

Beside it, there's a narrow strip of carpet. Barely wide enough for one.

Sam looks at the walkway the way you'd look at a bed. "Oh, thank God," he says. "Let something else do the walking for once."

You watch the ridges on the rubber slide past your feet. Smooth. Even. Towards you. Away from where you're going, and back towards where you came from.

It's running backwards.

Anyone tired enough wouldn't notice. Plenty of airports have walkways going both ways. You could step on, walk against it for a bit, let your legs stop thinking. It looks so gentle.

Sam is already reaching for the rail.

If you step onto the walkway, turn to {D02}.

If you pull Sam back and walk beside it, single file, along the strip of carpet, turn to {A34}.
D02:
You step on. You'll walk against it. You used to run up the down escalators while Dad pretended not to see.

The rubber takes your feet, and it holds.

You walk. You don't go anywhere. Soon you're only standing, and it's carrying you, gently, back. Past Gate 14. Past the kiosk, where the shutter rolls itself up and someone in a paper hat waves from behind the till, unblinking.

Through the windows the sky goes light and dark and light and dark. Past three years of *fine*. Past the day you left. It takes you back and back until you're small enough to be carried.

Then it sets you down on the viewing deck, on a Sunday, your nose flat against the glass, the planes all leaving. An arm settles round your shoulders in a grey wool sleeve.

"There you are," it says, and then your name, in a voice that is nearly his.

You never see Sam go. Only, a long time later, you notice that nobody is standing beside you.

The arm doesn't lift. The planes keep leaving. The afternoon never ends.

Add 1 to your Claim. Return to {A31} and choose again.
A34:
You haven't gone far when a klaxon sounds, one short blast, close enough to make you both jump. Ahead, an orange light begins to turn, sweeping the walls.

You come round the corner into a place that shouldn't be here. A baggage hall, in the middle of departures, where no baggage hall has any business being. Low ceiling. Rows of abandoned trolleys. A single carousel, its steel plates grinding into motion by themselves.

It comes round empty. Then not empty.

One suitcase. Old, hard-shelled, a dull brown, with a fat leather strap buckled round it and a paper tag on the handle: *LV 137*. It rides through the rubber flaps towards you, slowly. It stops, though the belt doesn't, the plates sliding on underneath it.

The strap unbuckles itself. Then the zip. From the inside. You hear the teeth parting one at a time, and you watch the pull tab travel along its track, and nothing outside is holding it.

A hand comes out through the gap. Grey. Then another. More fingers than make sense, feeling along the rim of the case the way you'd feel for a light switch in the dark.

"Nope," says Sam, under his breath. "No. Nope."

Whatever it is, it's unfolding. The case was too small for it. The case was never the right size.

If you stand your ground and see what crawls out, turn to {A35}.

If you grab Sam and run, turn to {A36}.
A35:
It comes out of the case the way a spider comes out of a plughole: nothing, then legs, then all of it.

It's roughly the shape of a person who was folded to fit and left folded too long. Grey and creased, in the rags of a travelling blazer, a dozen faded luggage tags tied round its wrists. Where its face should be, there's one of those little plastic windows from an old suitcase, the kind you slide a name card into.

The card is blank. It turns the blankness towards you. It wants it filled in.

You stood your ground long enough to see it. It drops off the belt and comes for you, low and fast, and you stop standing anywhere.

You run. You grab Sam by the strap of his backpack and haul, and the strap gives, and the bag skids away across the floor. Behind you, the thing patters over the tiles, quick and light and gaining.

You shove a trolley into its path. It doesn't slow. One of its tags snags on the handle, white and new, with your initials on it.

Ahead, a door marked *STAFF ONLY* is propped open with a fire extinguisher. Thirty metres. Test your Nerve.

If you succeed, you get Sam through first and kick the extinguisher clear. The door slams. Through its wired glass you watch the thing stop, and fold, and fold again, until there's nothing on the tiles but a brown suitcase with its strap done up. Turn to {A37}.

If you fail, it catches you short of the door. It gets into your collar and the corner of your mouth, and the little window presses cold against your cheek, reading you. When you tear free and fall through the door, the card isn't blank any more. Lose 4 Vigour and add 1 to your Claim. Turn to {A37}.
A36:
You don't wait to see the rest. You grab Sam's wrist and run.

Across the baggage hall, weaving between the trolleys, towards a pair of doors marked *NOTHING TO DECLARE*. Behind you something drops off the carousel with a soft wet slap, and then it's coming: a fast pattering, like a hundred fingers drumming on a table.

Halfway across, Sam's backpack slides off his shoulder. He twists back for it and you drag him on.

The doors are twenty metres away. Fifteen. The pattering is right behind your heels. Test your Fortune.

If you are Lucky, you hit the doors at full tilt and they swing shut behind you, and something thumps against them once, and then nothing. Turn to {A37}.

If you are Unlucky, it catches your ankle as you go through, a grip of cold wire, and you leave skin behind when you tear free. Lose 2 Vigour and turn to {A37}.
A37:
When it's quiet again, really quiet, the carousel stopped, the orange light dark, nothing moving anywhere in the hall, Sam goes back for his backpack.

It's lying face down on the tiles, and even before he turns it over you can see its shape is wrong. The fabric has been opened. Not unzipped. Opened, in long, careful slits, like a letter someone wanted to read without tearing the envelope.

Sam kneels and goes through it. Charger. A paperback. Washbag. And folded at the bottom, wrapped in a carrier bag, Dad's coat.

The long grey wool one, with the one button that never matched. He wore it on the viewing deck every Sunday. You'd know it in the dark by the smell. You didn't know Sam had it. You didn't know he was bringing it.

"I wasn't putting it in the hold," Sam says, to the zip.

You open your mouth. "You'd have checked it," he says. "Don't."

He stops talking. He goes through the bag again. Every pocket. The front one, the inside one, the little one with the key clip. A third time, faster. Then he holds it open and stares into it.

"They took my passport." His voice goes up and thin. "It's gone. They took my passport."

The coat is untouched. Everything else is untouched.

*If you have MARKED,* he goes through it all left-handed. His right fist, with the letter on the back, stays tucked inside his sleeve.

He looks up at you.

From somewhere ahead, past the far doors, comes a vast soft clattering: a thousand letters turning over.

Turn to {A38}.
A38:
Past the doors, the corridor opens into the Atrium, and you both stop walking.

It's enormous. Four storeys of glass and steel, the roof lost in darkness. Escalators climb to galleries that lead nowhere.

In the middle, hung on cables so long you can't see where they're anchored, is the great departures board. The old kind. Hundreds of black flaps and amber letters, turning over in waves, a sound like a flock of birds lifting off a roof, again and again, and never getting anywhere.

It settles, line by line.

You read the first destination and don't understand it. Sam sees it and makes a small sound in his throat.

*GLASSHAVEN. ON TIME.*

*PORT EVER. BOARDING.*

*SAINT UNDERMERE. DELAYED.*

*HOLLOWMOUTH. GATE CLOSED.*

*LANTERN BAY. CANCELLED.*

"Those are mine," Sam says. "Those are *mine*."

And you remember properly. Sundays on the viewing deck, Dad between you with a flask of tea, playing *Where are they going?* You made up lives for the passengers. Sam made up the places, better ones than the real ones. Glasshaven, where everything was made of windows. Port Ever, where nobody had to come home.

You had forgotten every one of them. Sam hadn't.

"Nobody knows those," he whispers. "Just us. Us and him."

Beside SAINT UNDERMERE the flaps stick on *DELAYED*, and before you can stop it you think of Dad's news, and how late it reached you: four months after the scan. Sam had known the whole time. He sees where you're looking, and looks away first.

One line doesn't move. Everything else flickers and clatters, but this line holds still, waiting:

*LV 137. FINAL BOARDING. GATE 0. 05:59.*

The time snags in you. Beside it, where the others say *ON TIME* or *DELAYED*, the flaps spell out:

*AWAITING 2 PASSENGERS.*

Sam turns his back on the cities. "Two," he says.

*If you have THAW,* he nods up at HOLLOWMOUTH. "You always wanted that one. Gate closed." A breath. "Serves you right."

Turn to {H01}.
